title: The Hymn of Vessel Farm
premise: Hospice nurse Marguerite Fairweather has spent years at Vessel Farm, a converted manor where the dying always count backwards from a number only they seem to know, and she records every death in her ledger as a private act of devotion. When the village's church bell—melted down in 1911—begins ringing each night, the counts accelerate, and Marguerite realizes the bell tolls once for every soul the farm has 'harvested' to keep its residents unnaturally alive. The last resident, ancient matriarch Odile Vessel, is preparing to sign papers that would bind Marguerite's family to the farm as its next keepers. Marguerite must unravel the ledger's true purpose, break the count before Odile signs, and choose between her own erased memories and her children's freedom—ending with the bell falling silent as the farm finally lets its dead rest, and Marguerite, half-remembered and half-new, walking her family out at dawn.
about_author: Yara Crane is the pen name of a former palliative care volunteer from the Norfolk coast who claims she never wrote fiction until a patient asked her to 'write it down so it stays true.' Her work blends clinical restraint with folk horror, and she refuses to attend readings held after dark.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Hours
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She introduces Vessel Farm's nightly rituals and her meticulous death-ledger, revealing the dying's backwards counting as a strange comfort. Emotional beat: quiet devotion shadowed by unease when her newest patient counts down to a number that hasn't arrived yet.

chapters.title: A Bell That Isn't There
chapters.summary: Marguerite hears the church bell at 3 a.m. and learns from groundskeeper Pell it was melted down in 1911. No one else admits hearing it. Emotional beat: the first crack in her ordered world; documentation suddenly feels like a prayer no one is answering.

chapters.title: Counting Backwards from Forty
chapters.summary: Patient Edwin Hallow begins counting from forty, one number per night. Marguerite cross-references her ledger and finds every resident once counted from forty. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professional diligence.

chapters.title: Odile's Papers
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Matriarch Odile Vessel summons her, offering guardianship papers that would keep Marguerite's family 'safe within the grounds forever.' Marguerite declines politely. Emotional beat: flattered, flattered, then cold—she glimpses the word 'succeed' in the margin.

chapters.title: The Children Who Don't Ask
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, home life. Her two children, Iris and Tam, have never once asked why they can't leave the farm grounds. She tests them; they answer in unison. Emotional beat: maternal terror beneath domestic calm.

chapters.title: Pell's Confession, Partial
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. The groundskeeper admits he hears the bell and has heard it for sixty years, always before a signing. He begs her to burn her ledger. Emotional beat: complicity wearing the face of kindness.

chapters.title: Forty-One Names
chapters.summary: Marguerite discovers the ledger predates her: forty-one entries in her own handwriting she never wrote. The oldest is dated 1911. Emotional beat: identity unraveling; the horror of being documented by yourself.

chapters.title: The Village That Looks Away
chapters.summary: Marguerite walks to the village; shopkeepers are warm but cannot say the word 'Vessel.' A priest crosses himself at her ledger. Emotional beat: isolation sharpening into paranoia.

chapters.title: Edwin Reaches Thirty
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Edwin's countdown continues; each night the bell tolls his number. He begins describing the bell's casting, a foundry he's never seen. Emotional beat: tenderness curdling—she is witnessing a possession by installment.

chapters.title: The Melted Bell
chapters.summary: Archival interlude, Marguerite reading parish records. The 1911 bell was melted to fund the farm; the foundryman's name matches a ledger entry. Emotional beat: history as a debt still accruing interest.

chapters.title: What Iris Drew
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Her daughter draws the bell, accurate to the crack in its crown, and says 'the lady under the floor hums it.' Emotional beat: a mother's denial breaking.

chapters.title: Odile at the Window
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, first time. She watches Marguerite's cottage and reflects on keepers she has outlived; she does not hate them, which is worse. Emotional beat: patient, ancient appetite.

chapters.title: The Hum Beneath
chapters.summary: Marguerite finds a sealed cellar stair behind the pantry. From beneath comes humming—the bell's note, sustained. Emotional beat: the house's body revealed as a throat.

chapters.title: Twenty-Nine
chapters.summary: Edwin's countdown. He begs Marguerite to let him finish, saying the counting is 'how we pay.' Emotional beat: horrifying consent—the dying choose this.

chapters.title: The First Keeper
chapters.summary: Ledger interlude. The 1911 entry describes Agnes Vessel trading her memory of her son to keep him alive past death. Emotional beat: the theme's thesis—the price of survival is who you were.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Missing Year
chapters.summary: Marguerite interrogates her own memory and finds a smooth, featureless gap where a year should be. Pell won't meet her eyes. Emotional beat: grief for a self she can't locate.

chapters.title: The Priest's Warning
chapters.summary: Father Anselm's POV. He tells her the bell rings for 'the unwritten,' souls traded without record, and that her ledger is the only thing keeping the farm honest. Emotional beat: her documentation reframed as a binding, not a comfort.

chapters.title: Twenty-Two and the Signing Date
chapters.summary: Marguerite realizes Edwin's count will reach zero on the day Odile plans to sign the papers. Emotional beat: the plot's clock becomes visible; dread acquires a deadline.

chapters.title: Tam Speaks in Numbers
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Her son sleep-counts backwards in a voice not his own. Emotional beat: the stakes turn from abstract to parental and immediate.

chapters.title: Pell's Whole Confession
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. He was the foundryman's apprentice; he poured the bell's metal and has kept the farm's count ever since, unable to die until it's paid. Emotional beat: pity for the complicit; he wants her to succeed where he failed.

chapters.title: The Room of Signatures
chapters.summary: Marguerite finds a chamber of framed contracts, one keeper per generation, each signature followed by a memory struck through in red. Her own name is already inked, waiting for a date. Emotional beat: fate presented as paperwork.

chapters.title: Eighteen
chapters.summary: Edwin's countdown; the bell now tolls audibly to the whole household, and residents begin standing at windows in unison. Emotional beat: collective uncanny, the farm waking.

chapters.title: Iris Remembers For Her
chapters.summary: Iris tells Marguerite details of the missing year—a hospital, a promise, a funeral song. Emotional beat: the daughter carrying the mother's memory is both salvation and heartbreak.

chapters.title: Odile's Offer, Restated
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She offers Marguerite a trade: sign, and the children forget the farm entirely; refuse, and the count takes them instead. Emotional beat: the antagonist's logic is genuinely merciful, which is the trap.

chapters.title: The Unwritten
chapters.summary: Marguerite descends to the cellar and finds the bell's remains buried in soil, humming, ringed by forty-one small graves without names. Emotional beat: confrontation with the cost made physical.

chapters.title: Fifteen Nights of Documentation
chapters.summary: Marguerite writes obsessively, restoring the struck-through memories onto the page. Each restored name quiets the hum slightly. Emotional beat: documentation as literal resurrection; hope with a mechanism.

chapters.title: Father Anselm's Price
chapters.summary: Anselm agrees to consecrate the ground but requires the ledger's final page—Marguerite's own entry—to be written truthfully. Emotional beat: she must document her own complicity to end it.

chapters.title: Twelve
chapters.summary: Edwin, near the end, tells Marguerite his number was never a death sentence but a payment schedule, and that zero means the farm 'calls in the balance.' Emotional beat: clarity arriving too comfortably.

chapters.title: The Missing Year, Restored
chapters.summary: Marguerite recovers the truth: she signed once before, a year ago, trading her husband's memory of her to save him from the count. He left; she stayed. Emotional beat: devastating—the invisible life was a chosen sentence.

chapters.title: Odile Unbound
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. With Marguerite's resistance, Odile's own traded memories fray; we see the girl she was before the first bell. Emotional beat: the monster revealed as the first victim.

chapters.title: Nine
chapters.summary: The household counts aloud now, residents and children together. Marguerite seals the cellar with consecrated earth; the bell's hum becomes a scream. Emotional beat: escalation into siege horror.

chapters.title: The Papers on the Table
chapters.summary: Odile presents the signing at last; the pen is in Marguerite's hand before she notices she crossed the room. Emotional beat: the horror of almost-consent, the body negotiating without her.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: Edwin reaches zero and dies smiling as the bell tolls a final time—but the count doesn't reset. It transfers. Tam begins counting from forty-one. Emotional beat: the gut-punch midpoint climax; the debt has found a new debtor.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Entry
chapters.summary: Marguerite writes her true ledger page—every trade, every silence, the husband she erased—reading it aloud over the graves. The struck-through names lift from the old contracts like ash. Emotional beat: confession as weapon; the turning of the tide.

chapters.title: The Unmaking of the Bell
chapters.summary: With the debts named, the bell's remains crack apart. Odile, finally able to die, signs her own release instead of Marguerite's and asks to be entered in the ledger last. Emotional beat: antagonist's grace; grief and victory entangled.

chapters.title: Pell's Last Night
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. Freed from his sixty-year count, he tends the grounds one final time and lies down in the foundryman's old shed. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace for the complicit.

chapters.title: The Farm Lets Go
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Residents who chose the trade are given the choice again; some stay willingly, and the farm, unforced, becomes merely a hospice. The house exhales. Emotional beat: melancholy resolution—survivorship without triumph.

chapters.title: What the Children Keep
chapters.summary: Iris and Tam remember everything, by Marguerite's choice; she refuses to trade their memories of her even to spare them grief. Emotional beat: the theme answered—she pays in full rather than in erasure.

chapters.title: The Last Signature
chapters.summary: Marguerite signs the papers one final time—not as keeper, but as witness—and the ledger closes itself. The bell's note sounds once, gently, like acknowledgment. Emotional beat: ceremony, release, the prayer finally answered.

chapters.title: Hymn at Dawn
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, walking her children out the gate at sunrise. She is half-erased, half-new, carrying a ledger with blank pages she will fill honestly. Behind her, the farm is quiet for the first time in a century. Emotional beat: bittersweet survival—the price paid, the self imperfect but her own.
